title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa
titleOriginal: 神奈川沖浪裏 · The Great Wave
medium: Colour woodblock print, from Thirty-six Views of Mount Fuji
creditLine: Impression held in the Department of Asia
labelText: Three fishing boats are caught in the trough of a wave whose claw of foam hangs over them, and behind it — small, snow-capped, perfectly still — stands Mount Fuji. Hokusai was in his seventies and had been drawing for sixty years. The blue is Prussian blue, a European pigment newly cheap in Japan, and the print's entire modern life begins with it. Thousands of impressions were pulled; this is one of them.
extendedNote:
It is not a painting and never was. Hokusai drew the design; a block-cutter destroyed the drawing in the act of carving it into cherry wood; a printer inked and pulled each impression by hand, one colour block at a time. The image exists in the plural, which is exactly why it travelled. It sold for about the price of a bowl of noodles.

The composition works by a single reversal: the wave is the mountain. Its crest occupies the place a peak would occupy, and the real Fuji is demoted to a small white triangle in the trough, so that a thing which lasts an instant is given the shape of the thing that lasts forever. The boats are oshiokuri-bune, fast craft that carried live fish to Edo, and the men in them are not drowning — they are ducking, in the practised way of people who do this every day. Prussian blue is the other half of the story: an imported synthetic pigment, arriving through the one Dutch trading post Japan allowed, which made possible a print built almost entirely out of blue.

regions.label: The claw of foam
regions.text: The crest breaks into fingers that reach over the boats — a shape Hokusai arrived at over decades of drawing water, and one that photography would later confirm as roughly what a breaking wave actually does. It also puts the wave in the compositional position of a mountain peak, which is the print's central joke and its central idea.

regions.label: Mount Fuji
regions.text: The sacred mountain, the subject of the whole series of thirty-six views, is here reduced to a small white triangle sitting in the trough, so far away that a wave can cover it. The permanent thing is made small and the momentary thing is made enormous. Every other print in the series argues the opposite.

regions.label: The boats
regions.text: Three oshiokuri-bune, the fast, narrow craft that raced live fish into Edo. There are eight rowers to a boat and they are not flailing — they are crouched flat along the thwarts in the practised posture of men who have met this before and expect to meet it again tomorrow.

title: Nebamun Hunting in the Marshes
labelText: Nebamun, a middling accountant of grain at the temple of Amun, stands in a papyrus skiff throwing a stick at wildfowl, his wife behind him in a pleated gown and his daughter crouched at his feet. A tawny cat — gilded eye, three birds in its claws and teeth — hunts alongside him. The marsh is a solid thicket of papyrus and the water below is full of fish drawn as though seen from directly above. It is a painting of an afterlife that looks exactly like a good day.
extendedNote:
The fragment comes from the walls of a small tomb-chapel at Thebes, hacked out in the 1820s by an agent working for the British consul; the tomb itself was never recorded and has not been found since, so these fragments are all that survive of it. They are among the finest painted surfaces to come out of Egypt.

Egyptian painting is often described as rigid, and the composition here is indeed governed by convention: Nebamun is larger than everyone else because he matters more, shown with his head in profile and his shoulders square on, and the register lines organise the world. But look at what happens inside the rules. The birds rising out of the papyrus are painted with an ornithologist's accuracy, species by species. The cat's eye is gilded — the only gold leaf on the wall — and it is looking directly out at you. And the whole scene is a pun: the words for throwing-stick, for the papyrus thicket and for the act of hunting all carry a second sense of creation and rebirth, so the picture of a man enjoying himself is also a diagram of resurrection.

title: The Admonitions Scroll: Scene Four
titleOriginal: 女史箴圖 · Admonitions of the Instructress to the Court Ladies
medium: Ink and colour on silk handscroll
dimensions: 24.4 × 343.8 cm overall — Scene Four of the nine that survive
reproduction: The scroll is three and a half metres long and was never meant to be seen at once: a handscroll is opened an arm's width at a time. What is reproduced here is the fourth of its nine surviving scenes, so its proportions are that scene's rather than the whole scroll's.

link.label: The whole scroll, at the British Museum

labelText: Scene Four: the toilette. Two court ladies at their mirrors — one kneeling to have her hair dressed by an attendant, the other seated before a bronze mirror on a stand, with her lacquer boxes open on the floor beside her. Nothing is happening, and that is the admonition. The text written alongside it says that everyone knows how to adorn their face and no one knows how to adorn their character, and the painter has answered it by making the grooming beautiful and giving the faces nothing to say.
extendedNote:
The scroll illustrates a political poem of about AD 292 by Zhang Hua, written to reprove an empress and framed as advice from an instructress to the ladies of the court. It is attributed to Gu Kaizhi, the first Chinese painter whose name and reputation both survive; what the British Museum holds is a copy made in the fifth to eighth century, which is to say a copy that is itself over a thousand years old and the earliest thing of its kind that exists.

Nine scenes survive of an original twelve. This is the fourth, and it is the one painters have gone back to: the mirror on its stand, the fall of a sleeve, the kneeling attendant's arm — done with a line the Chinese critics called "like a silk thread drawn from a cocoon", even in weight from end to end, laid down without correction and without shading. There is no background. The figures sit on empty silk, and the empty silk is the room.

The scroll was in the imperial collection for centuries; the Qianlong emperor kept it in a cabinet, added his own seals and a painting of an orchid, and it went into the Summer Palace. In 1900, in the looting that followed the Boxer uprising, an officer of the Bengal Lancers named Clarence Johnson took it home, and in 1903 sold it to the British Museum for twenty-five pounds — he had thought the jade toggle on the roller was the valuable part. It was then cut into panels and mounted flat in the Japanese manner, a conservation decision made in 1914 and regretted since, because a handscroll is an object you unroll, and this one can no longer be.

regions.label: The mirror
regions.text: A polished bronze disc on a lacquered stand, and the seated lady looks into it while the painter shows us her face directly. A mirror in this scene is the whole argument of the poem: it is the instrument of the thing being criticised, and it is also the only object here anybody is honest with.

regions.label: The hairdressing
regions.text: The kneeling attendant's arms and the fall of the sleeves are the line the scroll is famous for — even in weight from end to end, laid down in one pass, no shading, no correction. Chinese critics called it a silk thread drawn from a cocoon, and a thousand years of copying this scroll was a thousand years of painters trying to get that line.

regions.label: The empty silk
regions.text: There is no room. No wall, no floor, no horizon — the figures and their boxes sit on bare silk, and the bare silk does the work that perspective does in European painting. The text of the poem is written into it in columns, so the empty ground is also the page.

title: The Papyrus of Ani: the Weighing of the Heart
titleOriginal: Book of the Dead of Ani
dimensions: 42 cm high; the scroll runs 23.6 m — this is the judgement scene
creditLine: Acquired in Egypt by E. A. Wallis Budge, 1888
reproduction: The Papyrus of Ani is twenty-three and a half metres long and is kept, and shown, in separate sheets. What is reproduced here is one scene of it — the judgement — so its proportions are the sheet's rather than the scroll's.

link.label: The whole papyrus, at the British Museum

labelText: A man's heart is being weighed against a feather. Ani and his wife Tutu stand at the left in white linen; Anubis, jackal-headed, steadies the balance; the feather of Maat — truth, order, the way things should be — sits in the other pan. Thoth waits with a scribe's palette to write down the result. Beside him crouches Ammit, part crocodile, part lion, part hippopotamus, who eats the hearts that fail. Above, fourteen gods sit as a jury. The verdict is never in doubt in these papyri: the point of owning one was to have the right answer written down in advance.
extendedNote:
Ani was a royal scribe and an accountant of temple offerings at Thebes, and this was made for his burial around 1250 BC. What Egyptologists call the Book of the Dead is not a book but a spell list — the Egyptian title is closer to "the spells for going out by day" — copied to order for anyone who could afford it, with the buyer's name written into the gaps. Ani's copy is one of the longest and by a wide margin the finest: twenty-three and a half metres of it, the vignettes drawn by an artist who was allowed to take his time.

The scene reproduced here is the judgement, chapter 125, and it is the reason the papyrus is famous. The heart was the seat of the mind and the record of a life, and it is weighed rather than examined — an accountant's afterlife, which for a man who audited grain offerings for a living is not a coincidence. The spell beside it is a plea to the heart not to testify against its owner.

Budge bought it for the British Museum in 1888 and cut it into thirty-seven sheets for mounting, which is why it is shown, and reproduced, a scene at a time. The pigments are mineral: carbon black, red and yellow ochre, orpiment, Egyptian blue — the first synthetic pigment anyone made, calcium copper silicate, fired in a kiln at a thousand degrees a thousand years before this was painted.

regions.label: The balance
regions.text: The heart in one pan, the feather of Maat in the other, and Anubis on one knee with a hand on the plumb line. Maat is truth and order and the correct working of the world all at once, and weighing a life against it is the whole Egyptian theory of judgement in one image: not a trial, a measurement.

regions.label: Ammit
regions.text: Crocodile at the front, lion in the middle, hippopotamus behind — the three animals most likely to kill an Egyptian, assembled into one. She sits beside the scales waiting to eat the heart that fails, and a heart she eats is not punished but ended. Annihilation, not hell.

regions.label: The jury
regions.text: Fourteen gods on mats along the top of the sheet, each to be named and addressed in turn by the dead man, who tells each one a sin he has not committed. The list is the famous part: I have not stolen, I have not killed, I have not taken milk from the mouths of children, I have not stopped a god in his procession.

title: Portrait of Isabella Brant
medium: Black, red and white chalk, heightened with white, touched with pen and brown ink
labelText: Rubens drew his wife in three chalks — black, red, white — on a sheet the size of a sheet of paper, and it is the most direct thing he ever made. She is leaning very slightly forward, about to speak or having just spoken; the mouth is caught between two expressions. The eyes are worked hardest and the collar is barely there, four or five strokes of white over a hatched ground. It was drawn perhaps five years before she died, and there is no reason to think it was made for anything but himself.
extendedNote:
Isabella Brant was the daughter of an Antwerp lawyer and Rubens married her in 1609, the year after he came back from eight years in Italy with a reputation and a workshop's worth of ideas. He painted her often — in the honeysuckle bower beside himself, in the great double portrait made in the first months of the marriage — but the paintings are performances and this is not. It is drawn at conversational distance, on paper, at a scale that fits on a table.

The technique is trois crayons, three chalks used together, which Rubens took from the French and Italian portrait draughtsmen and pushed further than either: the red does the warmth of the face, the black does the structure and the hair, and the white is not a highlight but a light source, laid over both to lift the forehead and the bridge of the nose forward. Pen and ink sharpen the eyes at the very end, and that is the only place in the sheet where the line is hard.

She died in 1626, probably of plague, at thirty-four. Rubens wrote to a friend in Paris a year later, in the flat voice of somebody who has decided not to be eloquent: "I have lost an excellent companion, whom one could love — indeed had to love, with good reason — as having none of the faults of her sex." He remarried four years later, to Helena Fourment, who was sixteen. The drawing stayed in his house.

regions.label: The eyes
regions.text: The only hard line in the sheet. Everything else is chalk laid in hatching and rubbed, and then at the end Rubens takes a pen and brown ink to the lids and the pupils — which is why, at any distance, the face finds you before the rest of the drawing arrives.

regions.label: The mouth
regions.text: Caught between two expressions, which is a thing chalk can do and paint mostly cannot: the corners are left unresolved, two possible mouths drawn faintly over each other, and the eye settles on whichever one it expects. She is about to speak, or has just spoken, depending on how long you look.

regions.label: The collar
regions.text: Four or five strokes of white over the hatched ground and a lace collar exists. Rubens spends nothing here, and the economy is the point: the drawing is finished exactly where his interest stops, which is at her face.

title: The Flyer
medium: Watercolour over graphite, touched with white and gold, on paper
labelText: A man caught mid-step, one arm raised, the other hand open, a bird's wing tied into his hair and a pouch at his hip — inscribed by White himself, in the corner, “The flyer.” He is a Secotan priest or conjuror, drawn from life on the Roanoke voyage of 1585. The paper is otherwise empty: no ground, no horizon, nothing but the figure and his own shadow of colour. White sailed as the expedition's artist and came back with the earliest European eyewitness record of the peoples, plants and animals of the American east coast.
extendedNote:
John White went to Roanoke in 1585 with the job of recording what was there, and he did it the way a surveyor does: one thing at a time, on blank paper, without arranging it into a scene. A fish, a crab, a village, a woman carrying a child, a man dancing. The drawings are quiet and exact, and their emptiness is the point — there is no allegory in them and nothing is made to look strange.

This sheet is the one he labelled “The flyer.” The figure is a Secotan religious specialist; the English word White reached for was the closest he had for what he had watched. The bird's wing in the hair, the fringed apron, the pouch, the position of the hands — all of it is set down as information, and much of what is known today about Algonquian dress in the 1580s is known because he drew it.

What happened next to the drawings matters as much as their making. Theodor de Bry engraved them in Frankfurt in 1590 for a printed edition of Thomas Harriot's report on Virginia, and it was the engravings, not these watercolours, that Europe saw — with muscles classicised, poses corrected toward antique sculpture, and backgrounds invented behind the figures. The originals stayed in private hands, survived a warehouse fire in 1865 and reached the British Museum with the water stains still on them. Set the two side by side and the distance between observation and the picture Europe formed of America is measurable in inches.

title: A Lady, called Anne Boleyn
medium: Black and coloured chalks on pale pink prepared paper
creditLine: Department of Prints and Drawings, acquired 1975
labelText: A woman in an undercap and a plain gown, drawn from life in black and coloured chalks on paper the colour of skin. Holbein has done the eyes, the mouth and the line of the jaw and left almost everything else — the cap is a few strokes, the shoulders barely stated, the pink of the paper doing the work of the flesh. It is a working drawing, made at close range and quickly, of the kind he used as the record to paint from later. To the left of her, a hand a century younger has written in brown ink: Anna Bullen decollata fuit Londini 19 May 1536. Anne Boleyn was beheaded in London, the 19th of May 1536. That sentence is the only reason anyone calls this her, and it was written by somebody who was not born when she died.
extendedNote:
Holbein came to England in 1526 with a letter from Erasmus, went home to Basel, came back in 1532 and stayed. By 1536 he was the King's Painter, and the way he worked was this: one sitting with the subject, an hour or two, a sheet of paper prepared with a pale pink ground, black chalk for the structure and coloured chalks for the eyes and the mouth — then the sitter left, and the painting was made in the workshop from the drawing. Around eighty of these sheets survive. Most of the paintings they were made for do not.

So the drawings are not studies in the ordinary sense. They are the primary record — the only place a good many Tudor faces still exist — and they were drawn to be sufficient on their own: measured, unflattering, and made in one pass because there was no second sitting to be had. What looks like modern economy is a working constraint. Holbein put down what he would need and nothing he would not. The sitter here is in a linen undercap, the thing worn beneath a hood, which is to say she is drawn undressed by court standards — an argument used on both sides: a queen does not sit like this, or a queen who has known the painter for four years might.

The name came later, and not by much less than a century. The inscription is in a seventeenth-century hand, in brown ink, and it does not simply name her — it records the execution and the date, the way you would label a relic. Anne Boleyn was beheaded in May 1536 and comprehensively removed afterwards: her badges chiselled out, her portraits taken down, her daughter's mother made into a subject one did not raise. There is no undisputed likeness of her from life. The famous image — the gable hood, the pearl B at the throat — comes from Elizabethan copies of a lost original, made half a century on, when it had become safe to have one again. Which leaves this sheet: a face drawn from life by the best draughtsman in England, in the right years, in the right city, with the right name attached to it a hundred years too late by somebody working from what he had been told. It is either the only thing we have of her, or it is somebody else entirely, and the drawing is not going to say.

regions.label: The inscription
regions.text: Anna Bullen decollata fuit Londini 19 May 1536 — Anne Boleyn was beheaded in London, the 19th of May 1536. Brown ink, a seventeenth-century hand, added to the left of the sitter by somebody a hundred years after the fact. It is the whole attribution, and notice what it is interested in: not who she was, but how she ended. Somebody labelling a drawing as evidence of a death.

regions.label: The eyes
regions.text: Coloured chalk, and the only part of the sheet Holbein finishes. He is drawing against a clock — one sitting, then the sitter is gone — so the order of work is the order of what he cannot reconstruct later. A cap can be remembered. The set of somebody's eyelids cannot.

regions.label: The pink ground
regions.text: The paper is prepared with a pale pink priming, and it is not a background — it is the flesh. Holbein draws the shadows and leaves the lights untouched, so the ground itself does the cheek and the forehead and the throat. Everything below the jaw is simply the sheet, and the drawing stops the instant it has what it came for.

link.label: The sheet, at the British Museum

title: Bijan and Farud
titleOriginal: بیژن و فرود · a folio from the Shahnama, the Book of Kings
medium: Opaque watercolour, ink and gold on paper
dimensions: a single folio from a dispersed manuscript
reproduction: A Shahnama picture is not a picture on its own: it sits in a page, among ruled panels of verse, and photographers crop it in different places — some at the painted edge, some at the edge of the folio. Its proportions here are the photographer's decision rather than the book's.

link.label: The folio, at the British Museum

labelText: A duel on a mountainside, painted in Shiraz about 1437. Farud, in his father's fortress above, has shot the horse out from under Bijan, and Bijan is coming up the slope on foot with his sword out. The rocks are lobed and pink and stacked like clouds; the sky is a flat sheet of gold; the figures are the same size whether they are near or far, because distance in this tradition is height on the page rather than size. Above and below the painting, ruled in panels, the verse this illustrates goes on in six columns. The picture is not an illustration set beside the text — it is a widening of the text, made in the same ink, on the same sheet.
extendedNote:
The Shahnama is Firdausi's, finished about 1010: some fifty thousand couplets carrying Iran from the first king to the Arab conquest, written in a Persian that deliberately kept out as much Arabic as it could. It is the founding book of the language, and for five hundred years afterwards copying and illustrating it was an industry. There are hundreds of illustrated Shahnamas. This is a page out of one of them.

Shiraz in the 1430s was the place that made them at volume. Ibrahim Sultan, the Timurid prince who governed the city, kept a workshop of real ambition until his death in 1435; what followed was a commercial trade in manuscripts produced more or less to a pattern, and the pattern is what you are looking at. A high horizon with a band of gold sky. Rocks drawn as lobed, overlapping outcrops in pink and mauve. Figures tall, small-headed, arranged in a shallow band with no overlap you have to work out. No perspective, no cast shadow, no modelling — because none of it is wanted. A page of a book is a flat thing and the painting agrees to stay flat.

The episode is one of the cruellest in the poem. Farud is the son of Siyavush and the half-brother of Kay Khusraw, the king the Iranian army is marching for. He comes out onto the mountain above Kalat to watch that army pass, meaning to join it. Tus, who commands it and who is proud and stupid, takes the watching as an insult and sends men up to kill him. Farud kills two of them. Then Bijan, son of Giv, goes up; Farud shoots his horse; Bijan keeps climbing on foot, and Farud falls back into the fortress — where, shortly, he is cut down. The Iranians have killed the king's brother out of nothing but temper, and the poem knows it. What the painter has chosen is not the death. It is the moment before it, with the horse already down and everybody still alive.

The blue is lapis lazuli, ground from stone quarried in Badakhshan and carried west along the same roads that took it to Venice, where it was called ultramarine because it came from over the sea. The gold is leaf, laid down and burnished with an agate until it holds the light.

regions.label: The fallen horse
regions.text: Farud's arrow has gone into the horse rather than the man, and that is the whole of his position in the story: he is defending himself against people he came to join, and he keeps aiming low. The painter draws the animal's collapse with the same even outline he gives everything else — no strain in the line, no drama in the handling. The event is dramatic; the drawing declines to be.

regions.label: The rocks
regions.text: Lobed, overlapping outcrops in pink and mauve, stacked up the page like a cloudbank. This is the Shiraz convention of the 1430s and it is doing two jobs at once: it is a mountain, and it is the device that lets figures be placed higher on the sheet to mean further away, without any of them getting smaller.

regions.label: The verse
regions.text: Six ruled columns of Firdausi, in a hand that was on the page before the painting was. The scribe wrote the manuscript first and left the gaps; the painter worked into the space he was given. That is the order of authority in a Persian book, and it is why the pictures are almost always as wide as the written surface and never wider.

title: Vrindavani Vastra
titleOriginal: বৃন্দাবনী বস্ত্ৰ · the cloth of Vrindavan
medium: Silk lampas, woven in narrow strips and joined
dimensions: a fragment, some two metres across, of a far larger cloth
creditLine: Acquired in Tibet, where the cloth had been remounted as a monastic hanging
reproduction: The Vrindavani Vastra was never one object of a fixed size: it was woven in narrow strips and sewn together, cut apart again in Tibet, and what survives is a joined fragment of it. Its proportions are the seamstress's, not the loom's.
labelText: Bands of figures on a dark ground, woven rather than painted: Krishna dancing on the hood of the serpent Kaliya, lifting the hill of Govardhan on one finger, surrounded by gopis and elephants and lions, with lines of Assamese script running between the registers naming what is happening. Every figure is made of silk floats on a silk ground — no dye is painted on, no thread is embroidered over the top. The cloth was made in Assam in the sixteenth century, and it survived because somebody in Tibet cut it up and sewed it into a monastic hanging.
extendedNote:
The name means the cloth of Vrindavan, the forest where Krishna spent his childhood, and the weaving belongs to the Vaishnava revival that Srimanta Sankardeva led across the Brahmaputra valley — a movement that carried its theology in performance, song and textile rather than in temple sculpture. Tradition holds that the Koch king Naranarayana commissioned it, and that it took a workshop of weavers the better part of a year.

The technique is lampas: two warps and two wefts interlaced so that the figures are woven into the structure of the cloth rather than laid on it. It is done in muga and pat, the wild and cultivated silks of Assam, and the loom is narrow — so the design is built strip by strip, each one carrying its own band of the story, and the strips are then joined. That constraint is why the composition reads as registers: a horizontal narrative is what a narrow loom can make.

How it reached the British Museum is the interesting part. Assamese silk travelled north over the Himalaya as trade and as tribute, and in Tibet this cloth was taken apart and remade as a canopy or wall hanging for a monastery, where the climate and the dark kept it. Almost nothing of sixteenth-century Assamese weaving survives in Assam. What we have of it, we have because it left.

regions.label: Krishna on the serpent
regions.text: Dancing on the many hoods of Kaliya, the serpent who had poisoned the river. It is the moment the story is usually told at, and the weaver has given it the centre of a band and the widest spacing on the cloth — which in a woven design is the only emphasis available. There is no scale, no perspective and no shadow; there is position, repetition and interval.

regions.label: The inscriptions
regions.text: Lines of Assamese script run between the registers, naming the scenes. They are woven, not written, which means every letter had to be counted out in warp and weft before the shuttle moved — and it makes the cloth one of the earliest dated objects in the language.

regions.label: The joins
regions.text: The seams are visible, and they are two different histories. Some are the loom's: the cloth was woven in narrow strips and sewn edge to edge, because that is the width an Assamese loom gives you. Others are Tibet's: the hanging was cut down and reassembled for a monastery, four hundred years ago, by somebody who did not read the script and cared only that it was silk.

title: Sudden Shower over Shin-Ōhashi Bridge and Atake
titleOriginal: 大はしあたけの夕立 · Ōhashi Atake no yūdachi
medium: Colour woodblock print, from One Hundred Famous Views of Edo
labelText: Rain drawn as line. The downpour is cut into the block as two crossing sets of fine parallel strokes, laid at slightly different angles so the shower has depth, and the figures on the bridge hurry under it with their backs bent and their umbrellas tipped forward. The far bank at Atake has already dissolved into a flat grey band. Nothing in the picture is dramatic except the weather, and the weather is only straight lines.
extendedNote:
The bridge cuts the sheet on a diagonal from lower left to upper right, and everything else is arranged against it: the raft below, the dark water, the vertical rain. Hiroshige uses the bokashi gradation the Edo printers had perfected — ink wiped from the block by hand before each impression — so the river darkens toward the bottom edge and the sky darkens toward the top, and the lit band across the middle is where the whole composition breathes.

Van Gogh copied it in oil in 1887, squaring it up and surrounding it with a border of invented Japanese characters. He could not reproduce the rain: what is a single confident cut in the woodblock became, in paint, a thicket of brushstrokes. The print is the argument for the medium — a shower rendered by a knife in cherrywood, printed identically several thousand times.
